edges.effect_quant: The strongest quantitative studies point in a harmful direction, but the pooled magnitude varies across populations and methods.
edges.population: adults with long or late daytime naps
edges.mechanism: Long or late naps may reflect underlying illness or circadian disruption and can also fragment nighttime sleep, which is why their cardiovascular signal often looks adverse.
edges.summary: What makes this pair believable is not one flashy paper but the way the literature stacks up: the 2024 Wang meta analysis in PLoS One already points to long late-day naps tracks with higher risk or worse outcomes, and later studies mostly refine the size of the effect rather than overturning it. In practice this reads more like a real risk signal than a one-off finding.
edges.caveats: Residual confounding and reverse causation remain possible in some observational studies, so the main readout is direction and plausibility rather than one exact risk number.
